label: March 2026
blurb: The Supreme Court did more constitutional heavy lifting in one month than most years manage: a first-ever passive euthanasia order, a nine-judge bench on the meaning of 'industry', and an appellate mechanism grafted onto West Bengal's voter-roll revision. Parliament passed the Finance Bill and a contested transgender rights amendment in the same fortnight. topics.title: Supreme Court allows India's first court-ordered passive euthanasia
topics.hook: The Supreme Court let doctors at AIIMS Delhi withdraw life support from a man who had been in a vegetative state for twelve years, the first time a court itself ordered passive euthanasia rather than approving a family's plan.
topics.story:
Harish Rana was 32 when a head injury in 2013 left him in a persistent vegetative state. For twelve years his family kept him alive on clinically assisted nutrition and hydration, with no sign of recovery. On 11 March 2026 a bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K.V. Viswanathan ordered that support withdrawn, holding that CANH is a form of medical treatment and can lawfully be stopped once it no longer serves a therapeutic purpose and only prolongs a biological existence. Doctors at AIIMS began the withdrawal protocol and shifted him to palliative care.

This is not the moment India recognised the right to die with dignity. That happened in 2018, in Common Cause v Union of India, when a five-judge bench read the right to a dignified death into Article 21 and legalised living wills, or advance medical directives. The Court simplified that procedure in 2023, cutting out a layer of judicial officers and setting up a two-tier medical board system instead. What March 2026 changed is who applies it. Common Cause built the machinery for a patient's own prior wishes, expressed through a living will, to be honoured. Harish Rana had left no living will. The Court instead relied on its own inherent power and the medical board's finding of irreversibility to authorise withdrawal for a patient who never could have signed one.

The doctrinal path here is worth tracing because CLAT loves asking which case established what. In 1994, P. Rathinam v Union of India struck down the criminal offence of attempted suicide, reading a right to die into Article 21. Two years later, a larger bench in Gian Kaur v State of Punjab overruled that: the right to life does not include a right to die, the Court said, though it left open a narrower question about a dignified death for the terminally ill. Aruna Ramchandra Shanbaug v Union of India, decided in 2011 after nurse Aruna Shanbaug had spent 37 years in a vegetative state following an assault, permitted passive euthanasia in principle for the first time but required High Court approval case by case, and rejected active euthanasia outright. Common Cause in 2018 then generalised that into a workable, Article 21-based framework with living wills. Harish Rana is the first instance of a court invoking that framework to order withdrawal itself, without a prior directive from the patient.

The distinction CLAT examiners reach for is passive versus active euthanasia. Passive euthanasia withholds or withdraws treatment that would otherwise prolong life; active euthanasia involves a deliberate act, such as a lethal injection, to end it. Indian law permits only the former, and only under medical board oversight, and Gian Kaur's holding that there is no free-standing right to die still technically stands alongside Common Cause's dignity-based exception. A second familiar setup for a comprehension trap: distinguishing euthanasia from suicide, since Section 309 of the old Indian Penal Code (attempted suicide) was itself decriminalised by the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017, which presumes a person attempting suicide to be under severe stress rather than a criminal.

The ruling arrives as Parliament and state medical councils grapple with implementation gaps: hospitals unclear on how to constitute the mandatory medical boards, and no central registry yet for living wills despite the Court's 2023 simplification.

topics.title: Nine-judge bench reserves verdict on what counts as an 'industry'
topics.hook: A nine-judge bench led by Chief Justice Surya Kant spent two days on a single word, 'industry', deciding whether a 1978 definition covering everything from hospitals to gurudwaras still holds.
topics.story:
The question sounds narrow: what does 'industry' mean under Section 2(j) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947? The answer decides whether an institution's workers get access to labour tribunals, reinstatement rights, and protection against arbitrary dismissal, or whether they are left to ordinary contract and service law. From 17 to 18 March 2026, a nine-judge bench heard arguments on the point, and on 19 March reserved judgment, closing a question that had sat before the Court in various forms for over twenty years.

The definitional history is a case study in a court repeatedly widening a phrase and then hunting for a way to narrow it. In D.N. Banerji v P.R. Mukherjee (1953), the Court held that a municipal committee's sanitary department counted as an industry, an early sign it would read the term broadly rather than restrict it to profit-making commerce. State of Bombay v Hospital Mazdoor Sabha (1960) extended this to hospitals run by government, on the reasoning that organised activity involving cooperation between employer and employee to produce services for others is what matters, not who runs the enterprise or whether it turns a profit.

That logic reached its fullest and most contested statement in Bangalore Water-Supply & Sewerage Board v A. Rajappa (1978), decided by a seven-judge bench. It devised what is usually called the triple test: an activity is an industry if there is systematic activity, cooperation between employer and employees, and production or distribution of goods or services calculated to satisfy human wants or wishes, ordinarily rendered with a view to profit but not necessarily so. On that test, professions, clubs, and even some charitable and religious institutions with substantial paid staff could count as industries. The judgment attracted immediate criticism for being unworkable in practice and for sweeping in bodies, like hospitals and educational institutions, that Parliament arguably never meant to cover. Successive benches flagged the problems but lacked the numbers to overturn a seven-judge ruling, since Indian precedent requires an equal or larger bench to reconsider one. That is why the question needed nine judges this time, one more than Bangalore Water-Supply's seven.

Parliament tried to legislate a fix in 1982, adding an amendment to Section 2(j) that listed exclusions such as hospitals, educational institutions, and charitable bodies. That amendment was never brought into force through a notification, leaving the 1978 judicial definition as the operative law for over four decades. The nine-judge bench in March 2026, presided over by Chief Justice Surya Kant with Justices Joymalya Bagchi and Vipul Pancholi on the panel, examined whether that gap between an unenforced statutory amendment and an unworkable judicial test should finally be closed by the Court itself, and whether the triple test should be replaced with a narrower standard tied more closely to commercial or trade character.

The stakes are practical rather than abstract. If an employer is not running an 'industry', its workers cannot approach a Labour Court or Industrial Tribunal for disputes over dismissal, wages, or retrenchment, and instead fall back on ordinary civil remedies, which are slower and offer weaker protections. Universities, hospitals, gurudwaras with large staff, and NGOs running large operations have all litigated their status under this provision at various points. A verdict is expected to reshape labour litigation across sectors that assumed, on the strength of Bangalore Water-Supply, that they were covered.

topics.title: Supreme Court sets up 19 appellate tribunals for West Bengal's voter-roll revision
topics.hook: Facing complaints that lakhs of voters were struck off West Bengal's rolls without a proper hearing, the Supreme Court ordered the Election Commission to set up 19 appellate tribunals to hear their appeals before the state goes to the polls.
topics.story:
The Special Intensive Revision, or SIR, is the Election Commission of India's mechanism for cleaning up electoral rolls: verifying every entry, removing duplicates and the deceased, and adding new eligible voters. West Bengal's SIR, run ahead of the state's 2026 Assembly election, triggered a wave of litigation after reports surfaced of large numbers of names being deleted, with many affected voters saying they had no real chance to contest the deletion before it took effect.

On 10 March 2026, the Supreme Court directed the Chief Justice of the Calcutta High Court to constitute a bench of former Chief Justices and retired High Court judges to hear these appeals, and ordered the ECI to notify an appellate body for the purpose. It also directed the state government and the ECI to support the judicial officers running the SIR process itself. On 21 March, acting on the Calcutta High Court Chief Justice's recommendation, the ECI constituted 19 Appellate Tribunals across the state, one of them headed by former Calcutta High Court Chief Justice T.S. Sivagnanam and the rest by other former High Court judges, to hear appeals from voters excluded during the revision. On 25 March the Court verbally directed the ECI to resolve the backlog of contested cases before 6 April, and it separately held that persons whose names were deleted could not be allowed to vote in the 2026 elections while their appeals remained pending, a ruling that drew criticism from opposition parties who argued it effectively disenfranchised genuine voters during the appeal window.

The constitutional architecture behind all this is Article 324, which vests the 'superintendence, direction and control' of elections, including the preparation of electoral rolls, in the Election Commission of India, and Article 326, which guarantees adult suffrage for Lok Sabha and state Assembly elections to every citizen aged 18 or above who is not disqualified. The SIR itself is not a new invention: a similar exercise in Bihar ahead of its 2025 Assembly election drew a challenge from the Association for Democratic Reforms and other petitioners, who argued the process risked disenfranchising the poor and migrant workers who struggle to produce the required documents within tight deadlines. The West Bengal litigation follows that template closely, with the added edge of a border state where questions of citizenship and migration are politically live.

For CLAT purposes, the useful distinction is between the ECI's power to revise rolls (an administrative and constitutional function under Article 324) and a citizen's right to natural justice before being struck off them — the appellate tribunals exist precisely to bridge that gap, since the Constitution does not itself specify a hearing procedure for roll revisions and instead leaves the ECI to frame rules, subject to judicial review when those rules are seen to fall short of fairness.

topics.title: Parliament passes the Transgender Persons Amendment Bill, dropping self-identification
topics.hook: Parliament amended the Transgender Persons Act, 2019 to remove the self-perceived gender identity that the Supreme Court had made a constitutional right in NALSA v Union of India in 2014, drawing condemnation from Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch.
topics.story:
The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, 2026 was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 13 March 2026, passed there by voice vote on 24 March, cleared the Rajya Sabha the next day, and received presidential assent on 30 March. It amends the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019, which itself had been controversial for requiring transgender persons to obtain a certificate from a District Magistrate to have their gender identity officially recognised, a requirement critics said contradicted the spirit of the Supreme Court's 2014 ruling.

That ruling, NALSA v Union of India, is the doctrinal starting point for any question on this topic. A two-judge bench held that the right to self-identify one's gender, without any external medical or administrative certification, flows directly from Article 21's guarantee of dignity, along with Articles 14 (equality before law) and 15 (non-discrimination). NALSA also directed the state to treat transgender persons as a 'third gender' and extend reservations in education and public employment on par with other backward classes. The 2019 Act was meant to give legislative effect to NALSA but, in practice, reintroduced a certification requirement that transgender rights groups had spent years fighting.

The 2026 amendment goes further in the same direction that critics found objectionable in 2019. It redefines the category of 'transgender' more narrowly, removes references to self-perceived gender identity, and excludes several socio-cultural identities, including trans-masculine individuals, from the Act's protection. The government's stated rationale, presented during debate, was closing what it called definitional ambiguity that made implementation of welfare schemes difficult. Opposition MPs argued the Bill should have gone to a Standing Committee for wider consultation before passage, and pointed to the speed of its passage, roughly a fortnight from introduction to presidential assent, as evidence that scrutiny was bypassed. Amnesty International called presidential approval of the Bill 'a major step backward for human rights', and Human Rights Watch described it as a huge setback for India's transgender community.

For exam purposes, the essential comparison is between a judicially recognised right (self-identification, as constitutionalised in NALSA) and a legislatively defined category (the amended statutory definition), and what happens when the two diverge. India has no formal mechanism for Parliament to overrule a constitutional interpretation short of amending the Constitution itself; a statute that narrows a right recognised under Article 21 remains open to challenge before the Supreme Court on the ground that it violates the fundamental right the Court has already read into that Article. Expect litigation testing exactly that in the months following the amendment.

topics.title: Finance Bill 2026 clears Parliament, closing the Budget Session
topics.hook: The Lok Sabha passed the Finance Bill 2026 by voice vote on 25 March, the last major step in giving legal effect to the Union Budget presented at the start of the Budget Session in January.
topics.story:
India's Budget Session ran from 28 January to 2 April 2026, split, as usual, into two phases with a recess in between for parliamentary committees to examine the numbers. The Finance Bill is the vehicle that actually makes the Budget's tax proposals law: it carries changes to direct and indirect taxes, and unlike the Appropriation Bill, which merely authorises spending already voted on, the Finance Bill can touch substantive tax policy. The Lok Sabha resumed discussion on the Finance Bill 2026 on 24 March and passed it by voice vote the next day, after which it went to the Rajya Sabha, which cannot amend a Money Bill but can recommend changes the Lok Sabha is free to accept or reject. Parliament also passed two Appropriation Bills for 2026-27 and, on 17 March, an earlier Appropriation Bill, prompting Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman to assert that the government's budgeting remained transparent and realistic even as the Lok Sabha passed the roughly ₹45 lakh crore Union Budget for 2026-27 with limited floor discussion, a recurring criticism of how India's budget process actually plays out versus how the Constitution imagines it.

The constitutional scaffolding matters here more than the numbers. Article 112 requires the government to lay an annual financial statement, the Budget, before both Houses each year. Article 110 defines what makes a Bill a 'Money Bill': provisions dealing exclusively with taxation, government borrowing, or the custody of the Consolidated Fund of India, and crucially, the Speaker of the Lok Sabha has final say on whether a Bill qualifies as a Money Bill, a certification that is not open to challenge in the ordinary way. Article 109 lays out the special procedure for Money Bills: they must originate in the Lok Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha has only fourteen days to return the Bill with recommendations, which the Lok Sabha may accept or reject outright. This is why India's upper house, despite representing the states, has essentially no veto over the country's tax and spending decisions once a Bill is certified a Money Bill. Article 114 governs Appropriation Bills specifically, the instrument by which Parliament authorises withdrawal of money from the Consolidated Fund to meet the expenditure it has already voted through the Demands for Grants.

The Finance Bill 2026 also carried forward technical GST changes and completed the phase-out of the GST compensation cess, a levy first introduced in 2017 to compensate states for revenue lost in the transition to GST, and which had been extended repeatedly. Parliament also referred a separate Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 to a Joint Parliamentary Committee rather than passing it outright, showing that not every Budget Session bill moves at the same pace as a certified Money Bill.

topics.title: Iran shuts the Strait of Hormuz; US launches strikes to reopen it
topics.hook: Iran mined and blocked the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil passes, prompting a US aerial campaign to reopen it and a Security Council resolution, co-sponsored by India, condemning Iranian attacks on Gulf states.
topics.story:
The 2026 Iran war began on 28 February 2026, after the United States and Israel struck Iranian military targets, including an attack that killed Iran's Supreme Leader, Ali Khamenei. Iran's retaliation escalated through March: missile and drone strikes on Israel and on US bases in the region, and, from 4 March, a declared closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman through which tankers carrying roughly a fifth of the world's traded oil normally pass. Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps boarded and attacked merchant ships, laid sea mines, and warned vessels against transit. By 8 March, at least ten ships had been attacked and five crew members killed. On 19 March, the United States began an aerial campaign specifically aimed at reopening the Strait, deploying strikes against Iranian coastal and naval targets.

The Strait of Hormuz is one of the world's classic chokepoints, alongside the Suez Canal, the Strait of Malacca, and the Bab-el-Mandeb, and its closure sent oil prices up sharply, with knock-on effects for import-dependent economies like India, which sources a large share of its crude from Gulf producers. On 12 March, the UN Security Council adopted a resolution, led by Bahrain, condemning Iran's attacks on Gulf Cooperation Council states and Jordan, demanding an immediate halt, and reaffirming the sovereignty of the states affected. The resolution passed 13-0 with two abstentions and was co-sponsored by more than 130 countries, India among them, alongside Australia, France, Germany, Japan, the UK, and the US, a scale of co-sponsorship that signalled near-universal condemnation outside the immediate combatants.

For CLAT, the useful anchors are institutional rather than purely narrative. The Strait of Hormuz sits between Iran and Oman, connecting the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea; roughly a fifth of global oil consumption transits it on a typical day, which is why even a threatened closure moves markets. The Gulf Cooperation Council, founded in 1981 and comprising Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, and Oman, is the regional bloc whose members were the direct target of Iran's retaliatory strikes. OPEC, founded in Baghdad in 1960, includes Iran itself as a founding member alongside Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, and Venezuela, making Iran simultaneously an oil cartel member and, through the Hormuz blockade, a disruptor of the very oil trade that cartel exists to manage. And the UN Security Council's five permanent members, the US, UK, France, Russia, and China, retain veto power that a resolution like this one, aimed at a non-veto-holding target state, does not need to overcome; the tougher test in Security Council diplomacy is usually resolutions that touch the interests of a P5 member directly, which this one did not.

India's position, co-sponsoring condemnation of Iran while remaining a major buyer of Gulf oil and maintaining its own relationship with Iran through the Chabahar port project, illustrates the balancing act any question on India's West Asia policy in this period should expect to test.

topics.title: Maduro's second US court appearance, and the Monroe Doctrine's return
topics.hook: Nicolas Maduro, abducted by US forces from Caracas in January, appeared in a US court for the second time on 26 March, insisting he remains a head of state and 'prisoner of war' rather than an ordinary criminal defendant.
topics.story:
On 3 January 2026, the United States carried out what it called an extraordinary military operation in Caracas, deploying roughly 150 aircraft, an FBI unit, and the Army's Delta Force to abduct Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro from his compound, knocking out the country's air defences and causing a power cut across the capital in the process. President Trump framed the operation as domestic law enforcement, tied to long-standing US narco-trafficking charges against Maduro, while also pledging that the US would 'run' Venezuela and sell its seized oil, a statement that blurred the line between a law-enforcement action and a foreign regime-change operation. Maduro's first court appearance came in January; on 26 March 2026 he appeared again, continuing to argue that as a sitting head of state he was 'kidnapped' rather than lawfully arrested, a claim with no real precedent in US courts, which do not recognise head-of-state immunity for a defendant physically brought within US jurisdiction this way.

The episode is a direct descendant of the Monroe Doctrine, articulated by President James Monroe in his seventh annual message to Congress in 1823, which warned European powers against further colonisation or intervention in the Americas in exchange for the US staying out of European affairs. Over two centuries the doctrine has been stretched from a defensive statement into a standing justification for US intervention across Latin America whenever Washington judges its interests at stake, from the Roosevelt Corollary of 1904, which asserted a US right to intervene to preempt European intervention, through Cold War-era interventions in Guatemala, Chile, and Nicaragua, to the 2026 Venezuela operation. Venezuela itself carries a heavier symbolic weight than most Latin American states for this kind of confrontation: it renamed itself the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela in 1999 under Hugo Chavez, honouring Simon Bolivar, the early-19th-century leader who won independence for much of northern South America from Spain and is one of the region's defining anti-colonial figures. A US operation to remove a Venezuelan president plays directly against that founding mythology.

Venezuela's economic weight compounds the politics. It is a founding member of OPEC, the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries, established in Baghdad in 1960, and holds the world's largest proven oil reserves, larger than Saudi Arabia's, even though years of US sanctions and domestic mismanagement have collapsed its actual output well below capacity. The Organization of American States, founded in Bogota in 1948 to promote regional solidarity and non-intervention among its 35 member states, is the institutional forum where most Latin American governments have historically pushed back against US intervention in the region; how OAS members respond to the Maduro abduction, and whether the body condemns it or stays largely silent, is itself a live test of the organisation's relevance.

topics.title: Le Pen's National Rally surges in French municipal elections, then falls short in the big cities
topics.hook: Marine Le Pen's National Rally won more than 60 municipalities in France's two-round municipal elections and posted historic scores, but failed to capture Marseille, Toulon, or Nimes, the big prizes it needed ahead of the 2027 presidential race.
topics.story:
French municipal elections are held every six years for the roughly 35,000 communes across the country, and 2026's edition, held in two rounds on 15 and 22 March, doubled as the clearest stress test yet for the far right before France's 2027 presidential election. In the first round, more than 500 National Rally-aligned candidate lists cleared 10 percent of the vote, roughly twice the number that managed it in the 2020 municipal elections and a higher tally than the party's previous record set in 2014. Le Pen's allies won outright in Perpignan and built a strong lead in Nice, France's fifth-largest city, while running neck and neck in Marseille.

The second round, on 22 March, told a more mixed story. National Rally took control of over 60 municipalities nationwide and delivered what commentators called historic scores, but it lost the marquee contests: Marseille, Toulon, and Nimes, three cities it had specifically targeted as proof it could govern beyond its traditional small-town base, all went to non-National Rally candidates. Former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe won a key mayoral race for his own centrist party, one of several results read as a boost for mainstream rivals positioning themselves for 2027.

The National Rally itself carries a name change worth knowing: it was founded as the Front National in 1972 by Jean-Marie Le Pen, Marine Le Pen's father, and rebranded Rassemblement National, or National Rally, in 2018 as part of a long effort to shed the party's associations with its founder's antisemitic and Holocaust-denial remarks. Marine Le Pen has led the party since 2011 and has reached the presidential runoff twice, in 2017 and 2022, losing both times to Emmanuel Macron, whose second and final term under France's Fifth Republic constitution runs to 2027. The Fifth Republic itself dates to 1958, when Charles de Gaulle's new constitution created the strong-presidency system France still operates, replacing the unstable Fourth Republic.

For CLAT's comparative-politics angle, municipal results are a reasonable, if imperfect, proxy for national mood, but France's two-round system, in which a National Rally candidate can lead the first round comfortably yet lose the runoff once other parties consolidate behind a single rival, is the mechanism that explains why the party's vote share and its actual seat or office count can diverge sharply, a pattern also visible in French presidential elections.

topics.title: Nepal's Rastriya Swatantra Party wins a landslide; Balen Shah becomes PM at 35
topics.hook: Six months after Gen Z-led protests forced Nepal's prime minister to resign, voters handed a party formed only in 2022 a majority on its own, something no single party had managed in Nepal since 1999.
topics.story:
Nepal's parliamentary elections on 5 March 2026 followed directly from the political rupture of September 2025, when youth-led street protests forced Prime Minister K.P. Sharma Oli to resign, prompting an interim government under Sushila Karki, a former Chief Justice, to organise fresh polls. The result surprised even close observers of Nepali politics: the Rastriya Swatantra Party, or RSP, founded only in 2022 by broadcaster-turned-politician Rabi Lamichhane and now led by former Kathmandu mayor Balendra 'Balen' Shah, won 182 of the 275 seats in the House of Representatives, an outright majority. The Nepali Congress, one of Nepal's two traditional dominant parties, came a distant second with 38 seats, and the Communist Party of Nepal (Unified Marxist-Leninist), Oli's own party, took just 25. It was the first time since 1999 that a single party had secured a parliamentary majority in Nepal on its own, in a political system that had spent the intervening quarter-century cycling through short-lived coalition governments.

Balen Shah, a rapper and structural engineer before he became Kathmandu's independent mayor in 2022, was sworn in as prime minister on 27 March, eight days after the final results were confirmed. His cabinet, sworn in the same day, is the youngest in Nepal's history, and only two of its members carry prior ministerial experience, a striking break from a political establishment long dominated by veteran leaders from the Congress and UML.

The context that makes this result legible for CLAT is Nepal's own recent constitutional history. Nepal abolished its 240-year-old monarchy in 2008, after a decade-long Maoist insurgency and a mass movement, becoming a federal democratic republic; its current constitution, promulgated in 2015, established the current 275-seat House of Representatives elected through a mixed system of first-past-the-post and proportional representation. Since 2015, Nepal has cycled through numerous short-lived governments, none commanding a clear majority, which is the backdrop against which the RSP's outright win looks so unusual. Nepal's politics matters directly to Indian foreign policy: it shares an open border with India under the 1950 Treaty of Peace and Friendship, and Kathmandu's alignment between India and China has been a recurring theme, with Oli's government seen as tilting toward Beijing in his final years in office. How a young, untested RSP government under Balen Shah positions itself between India and China is likely to be one of the more closely watched foreign-policy questions in South Asia through the rest of 2026.

topics.title: Gaganyaan-1, ISRO's uncrewed test flight, targets its March launch window
topics.hook: ISRO pushed toward a March 2026 launch window for Gaganyaan-1, the first uncrewed test flight of India's human spaceflight programme, carrying the half-humanoid robot Vyommitra to rehearse the systems that will one day carry Indian astronauts.
topics.story:
Gaganyaan is India's human spaceflight programme, publicly announced by Prime Minister Narendra Modi in his Independence Day address on 15 August 2018. Its goal is to put Indian astronauts into low Earth orbit using an Indian-built launch vehicle and crew module, which would make India only the fourth country to achieve independent human spaceflight, after the Soviet Union (Yuri Gagarin, 1961), the United States (Alan Shepard, 1961), and China (Yang Liwei, 2003). The programme sits under the Indian Space Research Organisation, ISRO, founded in 1969 and headquartered in Bengaluru, building on the institutional legacy of Vikram Sarabhai, widely regarded as the father of India's space programme.

Before any Indian sits in the crew module, ISRO is running a series of uncrewed test flights to validate every stage of the mission independently. Gaganyaan-1, or G1, is the first of these, originally targeted for late 2025 and repeatedly shifted, eventually settling on a March 2026 window after spaceport scheduling constraints pushed it back. The mission is designed to demonstrate the full end-to-end sequence a crewed flight would need: characterising the aerodynamics of the human-rated launch vehicle, running orbital module operations, and executing re-entry and recovery of the crew module, likely splashing down in the sea for retrieval by the Indian Navy, mirroring how NASA and Roscosmos recover their own crew capsules. In place of a human crew, G1 carries Vyommitra, a half-humanoid robot built specifically to simulate an astronaut's physiological responses and operate onboard instrumentation, sending back data on life-support performance that engineers cannot fully model on the ground.

Two further uncrewed missions, G2 and G3, are planned through the rest of 2026 before ISRO commits to H1, the first crewed Gaganyaan flight, currently targeted for 2027 and expected to carry three astronauts to low Earth orbit for up to seven days. This is a deliberately conservative sequencing choice: both the US and Soviet human spaceflight programmes suffered fatal early accidents, and ISRO's insistence on multiple uncrewed validation flights before H1 reflects lessons drawn from those histories as much as domestic caution after ISRO's own setbacks, including the partial success of the Chandrayaan-2 lander in 2019 before Chandrayaan-3 successfully landed near the Moon's south pole on 23 August 2023, a date India now marks annually as National Space Day.

Gaganyaan is also a rare case of an Indian government programme with a specific, named human-rated launch vehicle: the Human Rated LVM3, an upgraded version of ISRO's existing LVM3 rocket (formerly GSLV Mk III), fitted with a crew escape system designed to pull the crew module away from the rocket in the event of a launch failure, a safety feature G1 is meant to help validate under real flight conditions.

topics.title: China's Two Sessions launch the 15th Five-Year Plan
topics.hook: China's National People's Congress opened its 2026 session on 5 March by approving the 15th Five-Year Plan and setting a GDP growth target of 4.5 to 5 percent, the country's slowest official target band in decades.
topics.story:
The 'Two Sessions', or Lianghui, are the back-to-back annual meetings of China's National People's Congress (NPC), the country's legislature, and the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC), an advisory body drawing in representatives from outside the Communist Party. In 2026 the CPPCC opened on 4 March and the NPC the next day, with Premier Li Qiang delivering the annual Government Work Report on 5 March; the sessions concluded on 12 March, the day the NPC formally approved the 15th Five-Year Plan, covering 2026 to 2030.

China's Five-Year Plans date back to 1953 and have been the country's central economic planning instrument through the Mao era's industrialisation drives, the Deng Xiaoping reform period that began in 1978, and into the present. The 15th Plan's approval matters because it sets the framework for China's economic priorities through the back half of the decade, at a moment when growth has structurally slowed from the double-digit rates of the 2000s. For 2026 specifically, Li Qiang announced a GDP growth target of 4.5 to 5 percent, a fiscal deficit ratio held at 4 percent of GDP, a consumer price inflation target of around 2 percent, and an urban unemployment ceiling of about 5.5 percent, figures that, taken together, signal a government managing a deliberate deceleration rather than chasing the high-growth numbers China posted in earlier decades.

For CLAT's comparative-institutions angle, the useful contrast is with India's own Parliament. The NPC, with nearly 3,000 delegates, is formally China's highest organ of state power and technically holds the power to elect the President and approve the budget, but in practice functions as a ratifying body for decisions already made within the Communist Party's own structures, unlike India's Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha, where floor votes, opposition scrutiny, and genuine multi-party contestation shape outcomes even when a government commands a comfortable majority. China's paramount leader, Xi Jinping, holds three formal positions simultaneously: General Secretary of the Communist Party (since 2012), President of the People's Republic of China (since 2013), and Chairman of the Central Military Commission, a concentration of civilian, state, and military authority in one person that has no real equivalent in India's separation of the roles of Prime Minister, President, and the constitutionally distinct chain of military command running through the President as Supreme Commander under Article 53.

topics.title: The 11th Raisina Dialogue brings 110 countries to Delhi
topics.hook: India's flagship geopolitics conference drew around 2,700 participants from 110 countries to New Delhi, with Finland's President delivering the keynote under the theme 'Samskara: Assertion, Accommodation, Advancement'.
topics.story:
The Raisina Dialogue is India's annual flagship conference on geopolitics and geoeconomics, held in New Delhi since 2016, jointly organised by the Ministry of External Affairs and the Observer Research Foundation, a New Delhi-based think tank. It is explicitly modelled on the Shangri-La Dialogue, Asia's premier defence and security forum, hosted annually in Singapore since 2002 by the International Institute for Strategic Studies, and is named after Raisina Hill, the seat of the Indian government in New Delhi where the Rashtrapati Bhavan and the Secretariat buildings stand.

The 11th edition, held from 5 to 7 March 2026, brought together roughly 2,700 participants from 110 countries, inaugurated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, with Finland's President Alexander Stubb delivering the keynote address as the Dialogue's Chief Guest. The theme, 'Samskara: Assertion, Accommodation, Advancement,' drew on a Sanskrit term for a process of refinement, framed by organisers as describing how a nation-state moves toward greater capability and clearer purpose. External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar, delivering the vote of thanks at the inaugural session, said discussions would centre on emerging capabilities, new strategic mindsets, and reassessing long-held assumptions in a rapidly shifting global order, with particular emphasis on artificial intelligence and its effect on strategic competition. President Stubb argued that the Global South would shape the future world order, with India in a central leadership role, a framing consistent with how Indian officials have positioned the country's foreign policy through the 2020s, positioning itself as a bridge between developed and developing-world blocs rather than firmly inside either camp.

topics.title: Paris hosts the second World Nuclear Energy Summit
topics.hook: France and the IAEA co-hosted the second World Nuclear Energy Summit, where Belgium, Brazil, China, and Italy joined 38 other countries in endorsing a declaration to triple global nuclear capacity by 2050.
topics.story:
The World Nuclear Energy Summit, held in Paris on 10 March 2026 and co-hosted by the French government and the International Atomic Energy Agency, was the second edition of a summit format that began in Brussels in 2024. Its central outcome was renewed endorsement of the Declaration to Triple Nuclear Energy, an ambition first announced by around 20 countries at COP28 in Dubai in 2023, committing signatories to work toward tripling global nuclear generating capacity by 2050 as part of the transition away from fossil fuels. At the Paris summit, Belgium, Brazil, China, and Italy formally endorsed the declaration, bringing the coalition to 42 countries, and major technology firms including Google, Amazon, and Meta, along with more than 140 nuclear companies, backed the government declaration with their own commitments, reflecting the surge in electricity demand from data centres and AI computing driving renewed corporate interest in nuclear power.

The IAEA itself, founded in 1957 and headquartered in Vienna, is the UN-affiliated body that promotes peaceful use of nuclear technology while monitoring compliance with non-proliferation commitments, a dual mandate that makes it central to any nuclear energy or nuclear weapons story. India is not among the IAEA's inner circle of nuclear-weapon states recognised under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, since it never signed the NPT, but it operates its nuclear power programme, including plants regulated separately from its weapons programme, under IAEA safeguards agreements specific to civilian facilities. India's own 2026 budget carried forward its Nuclear Energy Mission, targeting 100 GW of nuclear capacity by 2047, a domestic ambition that runs parallel to, though separate from, the Paris declaration's global 2050 target.

topics.title: Government declares India free of Left-Wing Extremism
topics.hook: Home Minister Amit Shah told the Lok Sabha that not a single district in India remains affected by Left-Wing Extremism, closing a chapter of insurgent violence that once ran through the 'Red Corridor' from central to southern India.
topics.story:
Union Home Minister Amit Shah announced in the Lok Sabha on 30 March 2026 that India had achieved a Naxal-free status, with the Ministry of Home Affairs subsequently confirming that zero districts remained on its Left-Wing Extremism-affected list as of April 2026. The number stood at 126 affected districts in 2014, when the current government first took office, meaning the reduction to zero took roughly twelve years, though the sharpest gains came in the final two, with 11 senior Politburo-level Naxal leaders killed and 5 more surrendering to rejoin mainstream life between 2024 and 2026 alone.

The insurgency being wound down traces back to a 1967 uprising in Naxalbari, a village in West Bengal, from which the term 'Naxalite' derives; the movement drew on Maoist ideology and, at its peak in the 2000s, controlled swathes of forested, tribal-dominated territory often called the 'Red Corridor', stretching in a rough arc from Pashupatinath in Nepal to Tirupati in Andhra Pradesh, spanning states including Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Odisha, and parts of Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh. The government's counter-strategy in recent years has run under the SAMADHAN framework, an acronym covering smart leadership, aggressive strategy, motivation, actionable intelligence, dashboard-based key result areas, harnessing technology, action plans for each theatre, and no access to financing, paired with heavy infrastructure investment, including over 15,132 km of roads built in former LWE-affected areas since 2014, more than five times the 2,900 km built in the years before.

topics.title: President approves a wide reshuffle of state Governors
topics.hook: President Droupadi Murmu approved a sweeping reshuffle of Governors and Lieutenant Governors across multiple states in early March, including new appointments to West Bengal, Maharashtra, Telangana, Bihar, and Himachal Pradesh.
topics.story:
In early March 2026, President Droupadi Murmu approved appointments and transfers covering Governors and Lieutenant Governors in several states and Union Territories. Shiv Pratap Shukla became the new Governor of Telangana; Jishnu Dev Varma, previously Governor of Telangana, became the 23rd Governor of Maharashtra on 10 March; R.N. Ravi, formerly Tamil Nadu's Governor, moved to West Bengal effective 12 March; Kavinder Gupta was sworn in as Governor of Himachal Pradesh on 10 March; Syed Ata Hasnain was appointed Governor of Bihar; and Nand Kishore Yadav became Governor of Nagaland. Rajendra Vishwanath Arlekar, who continued as Governor of Kerala, was additionally given charge of Tamil Nadu from 12 March.

Governors are appointed by the President under Article 155 of the Constitution and hold office 'during the pleasure of the President' under Article 156, nominally for a five-year term but removable, or transferable between states, at any time without the elaborate process that protects, say, a High Court judge. This flexibility has made large-scale Governor reshuffles a recurring feature of Indian federal politics, and a frequent flashpoint, since opposition-ruled states have periodically accused the Centre of using Governors as a political check on state governments, a tension the Sarkaria Commission on Centre-State Relations examined in the 1980s, recommending that Governors be appointed only after consulting the state's Chief Minister, a recommendation that is not legally binding and is followed unevenly in practice.

topics.title: Supreme Court orders a no-fault compensation policy for COVID vaccine deaths
topics.hook: The Supreme Court directed the Union government to frame a no-fault compensation policy for deaths that may have followed COVID-19 vaccination, while declining to legally attribute any specific death to the vaccine itself.
topics.story:
In Rachana Gangu v Union of India, decided on 10 March 2026, the Supreme Court addressed petitions from families who believed a relative's death followed COVID-19 vaccination, seeking recognition and compensation. The Court stopped short of holding any individual death was caused by a vaccine, a determination that would require case-specific medical causation evidence the Court was unwilling to presume. Instead, it directed the Union government to design a no-fault compensation policy, meaning claimants would not need to prove the government or vaccine manufacturer was negligent, only that death followed vaccination within a defined window, mirroring how compensation already works for some vaccine-injury and industrial-disaster claims elsewhere in Indian law.

The no-fault model has a direct precedent in the Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991, enacted after the 1984 Bhopal gas tragedy, which similarly allows victims of hazardous industrial accidents to claim compensation without proving fault. Grounding the direction in Article 21's right to life, the Court treated the state's mass vaccination campaign, and its encouragement or mandate of uptake in various contexts, as creating a corresponding duty to compensate adverse outcomes even without establishing individual fault, a reasoning likely to be cited in future public-health litigation.

topics.title: Taranjit Singh Sandhu becomes Delhi's new Lieutenant Governor
topics.hook: Taranjit Singh Sandhu, India's former Ambassador to the United States, took charge as Delhi's Lieutenant Governor in mid-March, stepping into a post that repeatedly clashes with Delhi's elected government over who controls what.
topics.story:
Taranjit Singh Sandhu, a career diplomat who served as India's Ambassador to the United States from 2020 to 2023, took charge as Lieutenant Governor of the National Capital Territory of Delhi in mid-March 2026. Delhi is not a full state; it is a Union Territory with a partially elected legislature, governed under the special arrangement in Article 239AA of the Constitution, inserted by the 69th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1991, which created the National Capital Territory framework and its own Legislative Assembly and Council of Ministers, while reserving 'land', 'police', and 'public order' for the Union government acting through the Lieutenant Governor.

The precise line between the LG's powers and the elected Delhi government's has been litigated repeatedly. In Government of NCT of Delhi v Union of India (2018), a Constitution Bench held that the LG is bound to act on the aid and advice of the Delhi Council of Ministers on matters within the Assembly's competence, except where the Constitution requires independent discretion, curbing what had been a broadly interpreted LG veto. A further 2023 ruling addressed control over services and bureaucratic transfers specifically, after which Parliament passed the Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi (Amendment) Act, 2021, and later legislative moves, to recalibrate the balance back toward central control over Delhi's civil service, a tug-of-war Sandhu inherits as LG.

The T20 World Cup itself began in 2007, with India winning that inaugural edition under MS Dhoni, a tournament often credited with accelerating the Indian Premier League's launch the following year. topics.title: India Climate Week and new 2035 emissions targets
topics.hook: India used the second India Climate Week to unveil interim 2035 climate targets, including a 47% cut in emissions intensity and 60% non-fossil power capacity, drawing criticism from environmental groups for lacking ambition.
topics.story:
India Climate Week 2026 ran from 12 to 17 March at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi, bringing together policymakers, industry, and financial institutions under the theme 'Prakrutirev Sharanam,' meaning nature is our only refuge. During the week, the government detailed its interim climate goals for 2035: cutting the economy's emissions intensity, meaning emissions per unit of GDP, by 47%, and reaching 60% of electric power capacity from non-fossil sources. These sit alongside India's longer-standing 'Panchamrit' pledges announced at COP26 in Glasgow in 2021, which include a target of net-zero emissions by 2070, a later deadline than most developed-country pledges of 2050, a distinction India has defended on grounds of historical emissions responsibility and per-capita fairness.

Separately, India moved toward operationalising its own domestic carbon market, the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS), enabled by the Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act, 2022, with compliance-market regulations adopted for rollout around mid-2026. Environmental groups criticised the 2035 targets as insufficiently ambitious given the scale of India's emissions growth trajectory, a criticism that echoes recurring debates at UN climate conferences over whether India's per-capita-emissions defence adequately accounts for its status as the world's third-largest emitter in absolute terms, after China and the United States.

topics.title: India and China hold border talks as China reasserts a Shaksgam Valley claim
topics.hook: India and China's Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination reviewed the border situation in March, even as China's earlier reassertion of a claim over the Shaksgam Valley kept tensions along the Line of Actual Control unresolved.
topics.story:
The Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination, or WMCC, established in 2012, is the standing India-China channel for managing border affairs short of full ministerial diplomacy, meeting periodically to review the situation along the Line of Actual Control, or LAC, the de facto and disputed boundary separating Indian and Chinese-held territory, which is distinct from a formally demarcated international border. The LAC has been the site of repeated friction points, most seriously the 2020 Galwan Valley clash, the first fatal India-China border confrontation in decades, and the 2017 Doklam standoff near the India-Bhutan-China tri-junction.

In January 2026, China reasserted a claim over the Shaksgam Valley, a region in the Karakoram that Pakistan ceded to China under a 1963 bilateral boundary agreement, an arrangement India has never recognised because it regards the entire Jammu and Kashmir region, including territory under Pakistani control, as its own sovereign territory. Against that backdrop, the two countries' border mechanisms continued functioning through March 2026, reflecting a broader pattern since late 2024, when India and China agreed on patrolling arrangements at Depsang and Demchok, of managing friction through continued dialogue even as underlying territorial claims remain unresolved.

topics.title: Gaza's ceasefire holds, unevenly, through March
topics.hook: The internationally brokered Gaza ceasefire remained formally in place through March 2026, but Israel continued operations against Hamas and diplomats kept pushing for the group's disarmament, with Gaza's Government Media Office logging thousands of violations since the truce began.
topics.story:
The ceasefire ending the two-year Gaza war, brokered with US, Egyptian, and Qatari mediation, has been in effect since late 2025 but has never amounted to a clean end to hostilities. By late March 2026, Gaza's Government Media Office had documented more than 2,073 violations since October 2025, including air strikes, gunfire, and incursions, while Israel continued targeted operations against Hamas even as diplomats pressed for the group's disarmament, a core unresolved condition of the broader deal. On 25 March, Israel's Coordinate of Government Activities in the Territories, COGAT, said it had intercepted engine oil, a restricted 'dual-use' item, being smuggled into Gaza inside UNDP aid crates, illustrating the kind of low-level friction that has kept the truce fragile without collapsing it outright.

The war itself began after Hamas's attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, and over roughly two years killed more than 72,000 Palestinians according to Gaza health officials, alongside tens of thousands of injuries, numbers that made the conflict one of the deadliest in the region's recent history. Hamas has also moved toward formally dissolving Gaza's governing administration ahead of an eventual, still-undefined transfer of power to technocratic administrators, a step observers read as an attempt to satisfy international demands for post-war governance reform without directly addressing the disarmament question that remains the ceasefire's most contested unresolved term.

topics.title: Russia's drone war intensifies as Ukraine fights to restore power
topics.hook: Russia launched more drones at Ukraine in March 2026 than in any earlier month of the war, even as Ukrainian forces intercepted 92% of them and worked to restore power capacity knocked out by earlier strikes on its energy grid.
topics.story:
Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, launched on 24 February 2022, entered its fifth year still grinding through incremental territorial shifts rather than any decisive breakthrough. Between 17 February and 17 March 2026, Russian forces lost roughly 33 square miles of held Ukrainian territory even as they pushed forward elsewhere, a pattern of gains and losses that has defined the war's static front lines for years. March 2026 saw Russia's heaviest drone bombardment of the war to date, though Ukraine intercepted 92% of the drones launched at it. On the energy front, Ukraine had restored only about 3.5 gigawatts of generating capacity out of more than 9 gigawatts damaged by Russian strikes on power infrastructure, with experts estimating that only 30-40% of total capacity might be restored before the following winter even in a best-case scenario.

Cumulative casualty estimates by early 2026 put Russian military losses, killed and wounded combined, at roughly one million, against 250,000 to 300,000 for Ukraine, figures that illustrate the war's grinding attritional character. NATO, the security alliance whose eastward expansion is one of the war's stated Russian grievances, and the Minsk agreements of 2014-15, which failed to hold before the 2022 invasion, remain the standard reference points for any question tracing the conflict's diplomatic backstory.

Bangladesh's 13th National Parliament began its inaugural session in March 2026, following a general election held in February that produced a decisive win for the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), which secured nearly two-thirds of the seats, while the newly formed National Citizens Party, built out of the 2024 protest movement, won only six seats. The BNP's return to dominance ends a political drought stretching back to the Hasina-led Awami League's long run in power, and puts the party, historically associated with a more India-cautious foreign policy than the Awami League, in charge of a relationship India has watched closely since 2024, given Bangladesh's importance as a neighbour, a major garment-export economy, and a country India shares its longest international land border with, at over 4,000 kilometres.

topics.title: GST collections cross ₹1.78 lakh crore as the cess winds down
topics.hook: March 2026 GST collections reached about ₹1.78 lakh crore, up 8.2% year-on-year, as the government completed the phase-out of the GST compensation cess first introduced in 2017.
topics.story:
The Goods and Services Tax, launched on 1 July 2017 through the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016, replaced a tangle of central and state indirect taxes, including excise duty, service tax, and VAT, with a single nationwide tax structure administered through the GST Council under Article 279A. Monthly collections are a routinely tracked economic indicator, and March 2026's figure of roughly ₹1.78 lakh crore, an 8.2% rise over the year before, came as the government wound down the GST compensation cess, a levy on top of GST rates on select goods like tobacco and automobiles, originally meant to compensate states for revenue shortfalls during the tax's five-year transition period but repeatedly extended beyond its original 2022 sunset date.

The GST Council, chaired by the Union Finance Minister and comprising state finance ministers, is the constitutional body under Article 279A that sets GST rates and structure by a weighted voting mechanism giving the Centre one-third weight and states collectively two-thirds. The 2025-26 reform cycle had already simplified India's slab structure from four principal rates to two main slabs, moving most items previously taxed at 12% and 28% down to 5% and 18% respectively, a shift the government credited with supporting consumption and, indirectly, the kind of collection growth seen in March 2026's numbers.
topics.why: GST Council voting weights are a frequently tested static-GK fact, since the one-third/two-thirds split is designed so neither the Centre nor the states alone can dictate outcomes — a cooperative federalism mechanism CLAT likes to probe.
