passages.title: The first court-ordered withdrawal of life support
passages.passage:
On 11 March 2026, the Supreme Court ordered doctors at AIIMS, New Delhi to withdraw clinically assisted nutrition and hydration from Harish Rana, a man who had been in a persistent vegetative state since a head injury in 2013. It was the first time an Indian court itself ordered the withdrawal of life support, rather than approving a plan the patient's family had already agreed to.

The order rests on a line of cases stretching back three decades. In 1994, the Supreme Court read a right to die into Article 21 in P. Rathinam v Union of India, striking down the criminal offence of attempted suicide. Two years later, a larger bench in Gian Kaur v State of Punjab overruled that holding, finding that the right to life does not include a right to end it, though it left open the narrower question of a dignified death for the terminally ill. That narrower question was answered in 2011, when Aruna Ramchandra Shanbaug v Union of India permitted passive euthanasia for the first time, but only case by case, with High Court approval required each time. The framework became general in 2018, when a five-judge bench in Common Cause v Union of India read a right to a dignified death into Article 21 and legalised living wills, letting a person set out in advance which treatments they would refuse if incapacitated. The Court simplified that procedure again in 2023, replacing layers of judicial oversight with a two-tier medical board system.

Harish Rana had left no living will. He could not have: he lost the capacity to make that choice in 2013, five years before Common Cause created the mechanism. The Court's March 2026 order therefore did something new. It held that clinically assisted nutrition and hydration counts as medical treatment like any other, and that a medical board's finding of irreversibility, combined with the Court's own authority, was sufficient to order its withdrawal even without a prior directive from the patient. Passive euthanasia, withholding or withdrawing treatment that would otherwise prolong life, remains the only form the law permits; active euthanasia, a deliberate act to end life, is not legal in India under any circumstance.

questions.q: What is the main point the passage makes about the Harish Rana order?
options: It is the first Indian case to recognise a right to die
It extends the Common Cause framework to a patient who never made a living will
It legalises active euthanasia for the first time in India
It overrules Gian Kaur v State of Punjab
questions.explain: The passage's central point is that Harish Rana had no living will and could not have made one, so the Court extended the underlying logic of Common Cause to a new situation rather than simply applying an existing mechanism. Option A is wrong because Common Cause (2018) already recognised the right; option C is wrong because only passive euthanasia is legal; option D is wrong because Gian Kaur's core holding, that there is no general right to die, was never overruled, only narrowed by later cases.

questions.q: Based on the passage, which case first permitted passive euthanasia in India, even if only case by case?
options: P. Rathinam v Union of India (1994)
Gian Kaur v State of Punjab (1996)
Aruna Shanbaug v Union of India (2011)
Common Cause v Union of India (2018)
questions.explain: The passage states Shanbaug (2011) 'permitted passive euthanasia for the first time, but only case by case, with High Court approval required each time.' Common Cause generalised this into a standing framework with living wills; it did not introduce passive euthanasia itself.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is true according to the passage?
options: The 2023 revision increased the number of judicial officers required to approve a living will
Gian Kaur v State of Punjab held that Article 21 includes a right to die
Active euthanasia remains illegal in India regardless of the circumstances
Harish Rana had signed a living will before losing consciousness
questions.explain: The passage explicitly states active euthanasia 'is not legal in India under any circumstance.' The 2023 revision reduced, not increased, judicial officer involvement; Gian Kaur held the opposite of what option B states; and Harish Rana had no living will, as stated directly in the passage.

questions.q: The passage implies that a key legal distinction in this area is between:
options: Government hospitals and private hospitals
Passive euthanasia and active euthanasia
Living wills made before and after 2018
Article 14 and Article 15 claims
questions.explain: The passage's closing lines draw a direct distinction between passive euthanasia, which the law permits under conditions, and active euthanasia, which remains illegal outright. The other options are not distinctions the passage develops.

questions.q: Applying the passage's reasoning, which of the following patients would NOT be able to rely on the 2018 Common Cause living-will mechanism directly?
options: A person who signs an advance medical directive while healthy, specifying they refuse ventilator support if in a coma
A patient with terminal cancer who signs a living will days before losing consciousness
A patient who has been in a persistent vegetative state since before 2018 and never made a living will
A person who updates their living will after a change in their medical condition
questions.explain: This requires applying outside knowledge alongside the passage: the Common Cause mechanism depends on a person making a living will while they still have the capacity to do so. A patient already in a vegetative state before the mechanism existed, like Harish Rana, could never have used it directly, which is exactly why the March 2026 order was legally significant.

passages.title: Nine judges and the meaning of 'industry'
passages.passage:
From 17 to 19 March 2026, a nine-judge bench of the Supreme Court, led by Chief Justice Surya Kant, heard arguments on a question that has unsettled Indian labour law for over seventy years: what does 'industry' mean under Section 2(j) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947? The answer determines whether an institution's employees can approach a Labour Court or Industrial Tribunal over dismissal or retrenchment, or whether they are left to slower, weaker ordinary civil remedies.

The Court has widened the definition steadily since independence. D.N. Banerji v P.R. Mukherjee (1953) extended it to a municipal sanitary department; State of Bombay v Hospital Mazdoor Sabha (1960) extended it to government hospitals. The fullest and most contested statement came in 1978, when a seven-judge bench in Bangalore Water-Supply & Sewerage Board v A. Rajappa devised what is known as the triple test: an activity counts as an industry if it involves systematic activity, cooperation between employer and employee, and the production or distribution of goods or services meant to satisfy human wants, whether or not it is run for profit. On that reading, hospitals, educational institutions, clubs, and even some religious and charitable bodies with substantial paid staff could all qualify, a scope many judges and lawyers found unworkable in practice.

Parliament tried to narrow the definition in 1982, adding a list of exclusions, including hospitals and educational institutions, to Section 2(j). That amendment was never brought into force through the government notification the law itself required, leaving the 1978 judicial test as the only operative definition for over four decades. Because Indian precedent requires a bench of equal or greater size to reconsider an earlier ruling, only a bench of nine or more judges could revisit the seven-judge Bangalore Water-Supply decision, which is why the question waited so long for a hearing of this scale. The bench reserved its judgment on 19 March 2026, and its ruling is expected to reshape labour litigation across every sector that had assumed, on the strength of the 1978 test, that its workers were protected.

questions.q: What is the primary issue before the nine-judge bench, according to the passage?
options: Whether the 1982 amendment to Section 2(j) is constitutional
Whether the 'triple test' from the 1978 Bangalore Water-Supply case should still define 'industry'
Whether hospitals should be nationalised
Whether Labour Courts have jurisdiction over criminal matters
questions.explain: The passage frames the core question as whether the seven-judge bench's 1978 'triple test' remains the correct standard for what counts as an 'industry'. The 1982 amendment's constitutionality is not the issue raised; it is discussed only as an unenforced legislative attempt at the same problem.

questions.q: Why, according to the passage, did the question require a bench of nine judges rather than a smaller one?
options: The Chief Justice has discretion to use any bench size for labour law matters
Nine judges represents the constitutional minimum for interpreting any Article of the Constitution
A precedent set by a bench of a given size can only be reconsidered by a bench of equal or greater size, and the 1978 ruling was by seven judges
The Industrial Disputes Act specifically requires nine judges for any interpretation dispute
questions.explain: The passage explicitly states the bench-strength rule: a precedent needs a bench of equal or greater size to be reconsidered, and since Bangalore Water-Supply was a seven-judge ruling, nine judges were needed this time. There is no such general nine-judge constitutional minimum, and the Act itself does not prescribe bench sizes for the Court.

questions.q: Which of the following is true according to the passage?
options: The 1982 amendment to Section 2(j) was notified and is currently in force
The 1978 triple test does not require the activity to be run for profit
D.N. Banerji v P.R. Mukherjee was decided after Hospital Mazdoor Sabha
The nine-judge bench delivered its final judgment on 19 March 2026
questions.explain: The passage states the triple test applies 'whether or not it is run for profit', making option B true. The 1982 amendment was never notified into force (contradicting A); Banerji (1953) came before Hospital Mazdoor Sabha (1960), not after (contradicting C); and the bench reserved judgment on 19 March, it did not deliver a final ruling that day (contradicting D).

questions.q: The passage suggests that the practical consequence of a wide 'industry' definition is that:
options: More institutions and their employees gain access to Labour Courts and Industrial Tribunals
Fewer government hospitals can operate legally
Religious institutions must convert into for-profit companies
The Industrial Disputes Act itself becomes unconstitutional
questions.explain: The passage opens by stating the definition 'determines whether an institution's employees can approach a Labour Court or Industrial Tribunal', so a wider definition extends that access to more institutions' workers. None of the other options are claims the passage makes.

questions.q: Which piece of outside legal knowledge would most help explain why Parliament's 1982 amendment failed to actually change the law?
options: Money Bills cannot be amended by the Rajya Sabha
Many Indian statutory provisions take effect only once the government issues a notification bringing them into force, and a passed amendment without one has no legal effect
Constitutional amendments require ratification by half the states
The Supreme Court can strike down any law with a simple majority
questions.explain: This is the general statutory-interpretation principle the passage assumes readers can supply: passage of an amendment by Parliament is distinct from its entry into force, which for many provisions requires a specific government notification. None of the other options relate to why an already-passed amendment could remain legally inert for over forty years.

passages.title: Appeals against West Bengal's voter-roll revision
passages.passage:
West Bengal's Special Intensive Revision, the Election Commission of India's process for cleaning up electoral rolls ahead of the state's 2026 Assembly election, triggered a wave of complaints after reports surfaced that large numbers of voters had been struck off the rolls with little real opportunity to contest the deletion. On 10 March 2026, the Supreme Court directed the Chief Justice of the Calcutta High Court to constitute a bench of former Chief Justices and retired High Court judges to hear appeals from affected voters, and ordered the Election Commission to notify a formal appellate body for the purpose.

Acting on that direction, the Election Commission constituted 19 Appellate Tribunals across West Bengal on 21 March, one led by former Calcutta High Court Chief Justice T.S. Sivagnanam and the rest by other retired High Court judges. On 25 March, the Supreme Court verbally directed the Commission to clear the backlog of contested cases before 6 April, and separately ruled that voters whose names had been deleted could not be allowed to vote in the 2026 elections while their appeals remained pending, a decision opposition parties criticised as effectively disenfranchising genuine voters during the appeal window itself.

The constitutional basis for the Commission's authority over electoral rolls is Article 324, which vests the superintendence, direction, and control of elections in the Election Commission of India, while Article 326 guarantees universal adult suffrage to every citizen aged 18 or above who is not otherwise disqualified. Neither article specifies a hearing procedure for roll revisions, leaving the Commission to frame its own rules, subject to judicial review whenever those rules are found to fall short of basic fairness, which is the gap the appellate tribunals were built to close. A similar Special Intensive Revision exercise had already been challenged before the Supreme Court in Bihar, ahead of that state's 2025 Assembly election, in a case brought by the Association for Democratic Reforms.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of the 19 Appellate Tribunals described in the passage?
options: To conduct the 2026 West Bengal Assembly election directly
To hear appeals from voters whose names were deleted during the SIR process
To replace the Election Commission of India in West Bengal
To prosecute Election Commission officials for misconduct
questions.explain: The passage states the tribunals were set up specifically 'to hear appeals from voters excluded during the revision.' They do not conduct elections, replace the ECI, or serve any prosecutorial function.

questions.q: Which of the following can be inferred about the Supreme Court's 25 March order regarding deleted voters?
options: It guaranteed all deleted voters could vote regardless of appeal status
It created a tension between resolving appeals quickly and voters' ability to participate in the 2026 election while appeals were pending
It permanently barred all deleted voters from ever voting again
It transferred the entire SIR process to the Calcutta High Court
questions.explain: The passage notes the Court set a deadline to clear appeals while also ruling that deleted voters could not vote pending appeal, a combination that creates real pressure to resolve cases fast, which is exactly why opposition parties criticised the order as risking disenfranchisement in the interim. It does not permanently bar anyone or transfer the whole SIR process to the High Court.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is true, based on the passage?
options: Article 326 grants the ECI superintendence over elections
Article 324 specifies the exact hearing procedure the ECI must follow when revising rolls
The Bihar SIR exercise was also challenged in court, ahead of Bihar's 2025 Assembly election
All 19 appellate tribunals are headed by sitting High Court judges
questions.explain: The passage directly states the Bihar SIR exercise was challenged before the Supreme Court ahead of the 2025 Bihar election. Article 324, not 326, grants the ECI's superintendence power; neither article specifies a hearing procedure, per the passage; and the tribunals are headed by former, not sitting, High Court judges.

questions.q: The passage's discussion of Articles 324 and 326 mainly serves to:
options: Show that the Constitution provides a complete, detailed appeals procedure for roll revisions
Explain the constitutional basis for the ECI's authority and the citizen's right to vote, while noting a procedural gap between the two
Argue that the ECI has no legal authority to revise electoral rolls at all
Demonstrate that Article 324 and Article 326 are identical in scope
questions.explain: The passage uses the two Articles to establish, respectively, the ECI's power (324) and the citizen's suffrage right (326), then explicitly notes 'Neither article specifies a hearing procedure', which is the gap the appellate tribunals address. It does not claim the Constitution is silent on the ECI's authority, nor that the two Articles are identical.

questions.q: A student familiar with the doctrine of natural justice would most likely connect it to which part of this passage?
options: The GDP growth figures of West Bengal
The requirement that voters get a genuine opportunity to contest their deletion from the rolls before it takes final effect
The appointment process for Supreme Court judges
The size of India's Parliament
questions.explain: Natural justice, the principle that a person should get a fair hearing before an adverse decision affecting them, is exactly the concern animating the original complaints described in the passage: that voters were struck off with little real chance to contest it. None of the other options relate to that doctrine.

passages.title: Closing a chokepoint: the Strait of Hormuz in 2026
passages.passage:
The 2026 Iran war began on 28 February, when the United States and Israel struck Iranian military targets, including a strike that killed Iran's Supreme Leader, Ali Khamenei. Iran retaliated through March with missile and drone strikes on Israel and on US bases in the region, and, from 4 March, a declared closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman through which roughly a fifth of the world's traded oil normally passes. Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps boarded and attacked merchant ships and laid sea mines; by 8 March, at least ten vessels had been attacked and five crew members killed. On 19 March, the United States began an aerial campaign specifically aimed at reopening the Strait.

The closure sent oil prices sharply upward, with direct consequences for import-dependent economies like India, which draws a large share of its crude from Gulf producers. On 12 March, the UN Security Council adopted a resolution, led by Bahrain, condemning Iran's attacks on Gulf Cooperation Council states and Jordan and demanding an immediate halt. The resolution passed 13-0 with two abstentions and was co-sponsored by more than 130 countries, India among them, a scale of co-sponsorship reflecting near-universal condemnation outside the immediate combatants.

India's position illustrates a familiar balancing act in its West Asia policy. It co-sponsored a resolution condemning Iran while remaining heavily dependent on Gulf oil and while continuing its own bilateral relationship with Iran, centred on the Chabahar port project, which gives India access to Afghanistan and Central Asia without routing through Pakistan. Iran itself is a founding member of OPEC, established in Baghdad in 1960, which makes it simultaneously a member of the oil cartel whose interests depend on stable markets and, through the Hormuz blockade, the disruptor of the very trade that cartel exists to manage.

questions.q: What is the central event the passage describes?
options: A trade agreement between Iran and the Gulf Cooperation Council
Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz and the international and US response to it
India's decision to stop importing oil from the Gulf
The formation of OPEC in 1960
questions.explain: The passage centres on Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz from 4 March 2026 and the resulting UN Security Council resolution and US military response. India's oil dependence and OPEC's founding are mentioned only as supporting context, not the main event.

questions.q: Which of the following can be inferred about India's position from the passage?
options: India refused to take any position on the Iran-Gulf conflict
India sided entirely with Iran against the Gulf states
India balanced condemning Iran's attacks with maintaining its own economic and strategic interests in the region, including with Iran itself
India ended all involvement with the Chabahar port project because of the war
questions.explain: The passage explicitly frames India's position as 'a familiar balancing act': co-sponsoring condemnation of Iran while continuing its Gulf oil dependence and its own Chabahar relationship with Iran. There is no indication in the passage that India took no position, sided fully with Iran, or ended the Chabahar project.

questions.q: Which statement is true according to the passage?
options: Iran is a member of the Gulf Cooperation Council
The UN Security Council resolution passed unanimously with no abstentions
Iran is a founding member of OPEC
The US aerial campaign to reopen the Strait began before Iran declared it closed
questions.explain: The passage states directly that Iran is 'a founding member of OPEC, established in Baghdad in 1960.' The resolution passed 13-0 with two abstentions, not unanimously; the passage does not state Iran is a GCC member (and it is not); and the US campaign began 19 March, after Iran's 4 March closure declaration.

questions.q: The passage's mention of the Strait of Hormuz carrying 'roughly a fifth of the world's traded oil' primarily serves to:
options: Explain why its closure triggered a global oil price shock and drew international response
Prove that Iran controls the entire Persian Gulf region
Show that Oman is the largest oil exporter in the world
Argue that oil trade through the Strait is declining over time
questions.explain: The scale figure is given immediately before the passage explains the resulting oil price shock and the international reaction, establishing why a relatively narrow waterway's closure had such large consequences. It says nothing about Iran controlling the whole Gulf, Oman's export ranking, or a declining trend.

questions.q: A student who knows that the Strait of Malacca and the Suez Canal are also global maritime 'chokepoints' would most likely use that knowledge to:
options: Argue that the Strait of Hormuz is not actually important to global trade
Recognise Hormuz as one instance of a broader category of narrow, strategically vital waterways whose closure disrupts global trade
Conclude that India does not depend on any maritime chokepoints
Prove that Iran also controls the Strait of Malacca
questions.explain: Recognising Hormuz, Malacca, and Suez as members of the same general category, maritime chokepoints whose disruption has outsized effects on global trade, is exactly the kind of outside static knowledge the passage assumes readers can bring to strengthen their understanding of why the Hormuz closure mattered so much. None of the other options follow from that outside knowledge.

passages.title: Maduro in a US courtroom, and the doctrine behind it
passages.passage:
On 3 January 2026, the United States carried out an operation in Caracas that it described as extraordinary military action, deploying roughly 150 aircraft along with an FBI unit and the Army's Delta Force to abduct Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro from his compound, knocking out the country's air defences and causing a power cut across the capital. President Trump framed the action as domestic law enforcement tied to long-standing US narco-trafficking charges against Maduro, while also pledging that the US would 'run' Venezuela and sell its seized oil, a statement that blurred any clean line between law enforcement and regime change. Maduro appeared in a US court for the second time on 26 March 2026, continuing to argue that as a sitting head of state, he had been unlawfully kidnapped rather than lawfully arrested, a claim US courts do not recognise once a defendant is physically within their jurisdiction.

The episode is a direct descendant of the Monroe Doctrine, articulated by President James Monroe in 1823, which warned European powers against further colonisation in the Americas in exchange for US non-interference in European affairs. Over two centuries, the doctrine has stretched from a defensive statement into a standing justification for US intervention across Latin America, from the 1904 Roosevelt Corollary through Cold War-era interventions in Guatemala, Chile, and Nicaragua, to the 2026 Venezuela operation.

Venezuela's own history sharpens the confrontation. It renamed itself the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela in 1999 under Hugo Chavez, honouring Simon Bolivar, the independence leader who won freedom for much of northern South America from Spain. It is also a founding member of OPEC, established in Baghdad in 1960, and holds the world's largest proven oil reserves, even though years of US sanctions and domestic mismanagement have kept its actual output well below capacity. The Organization of American States, founded in Bogota in 1948 to promote regional solidarity and non-intervention, is the forum where Latin American governments have historically pushed back against exactly this kind of US action, and how its members respond to Maduro's abduction is itself a test of the body's relevance.

questions.q: What is the passage's main argument about the January 2026 operation against Maduro?
options: It was purely a domestic law-enforcement matter with no broader political significance
It fits within a long pattern of US intervention in Latin America justified by an expanded reading of the Monroe Doctrine
It was authorised by the Organization of American States
It ended Venezuela's membership in OPEC
questions.explain: The passage explicitly calls the operation 'a direct descendant of the Monroe Doctrine' and traces a pattern of interventions justified by its expanded reading. It notes the operation blurred rather than confirmed a clean law-enforcement framing, and says nothing about OAS authorisation or OPEC membership being affected.

questions.q: Based on the passage, why is Maduro's claim that he was 'kidnapped' unlikely to succeed in a US court?
options: Because Venezuela is not recognised as a sovereign state by the United States
Because US courts do not recognise head-of-state immunity for a defendant physically brought within their jurisdiction
Because Maduro has already been convicted in a Venezuelan court
Because the United Nations stripped Maduro of his presidential title before the operation
questions.explain: The passage states directly that US courts 'do not recognise' the kind of immunity claim Maduro is making once he is physically within US jurisdiction. The other options are not claims made anywhere in the passage.

questions.q: Which of the following is true according to the passage?
options: Venezuela was renamed the Bolivarian Republic in 1948
OPEC was founded in Bogota in 1948
Venezuela holds the world's largest proven oil reserves
The Roosevelt Corollary preceded the original Monroe Doctrine
questions.explain: The passage states plainly that Venezuela 'holds the world's largest proven oil reserves.' Venezuela was renamed in 1999, not 1948; OPEC was founded in Baghdad, not Bogota (Bogota is where OAS was founded, in 1948); and the Roosevelt Corollary (1904) came after, not before, the original 1823 Monroe Doctrine.

questions.q: The passage's description of the Organization of American States mainly functions to:
options: Prove that OAS has always supported US intervention in Latin America
Introduce an institutional body whose response to the Maduro abduction will test whether it can actually push back on US intervention, as it was historically meant to
Show that OAS and OPEC are the same organisation
Argue that Venezuela should be expelled from OAS
questions.explain: The passage's final sentence frames OAS response as 'itself a test of the body's relevance', implying its historical role has been to resist this kind of intervention, not to support it, and that this episode will show whether that role still holds. It does not equate OAS with OPEC or call for Venezuela's expulsion.

questions.q: A student who knows OPEC's full name (Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries) and its role as a cartel managing oil supply would most likely use that knowledge to understand which claim in the passage?
options: That Venezuela's OPEC membership is irrelevant to the current crisis
That the passage's point about the US pledge to 'sell its seized oil' has particular significance given Venezuela's role in a cartel meant to manage collective oil supply and pricing
That OPEC members are barred from having any political conflict with the US
That OPEC was created specifically to respond to US intervention in Venezuela
questions.explain: Understanding OPEC as a cartel that manages collective oil supply and pricing among its members sharpens the significance of a foreign power seizing and selling one member's oil unilaterally, which is exactly the tension the passage gestures at without spelling out in full. The other options are not supported by outside knowledge of OPEC's actual founding or function.

passages.title: A 41-year-old party's outright majority in Nepal
passages.passage:
Nepal's parliamentary elections on 5 March 2026 followed directly from the political rupture of September 2025, when youth-led street protests forced Prime Minister K.P. Sharma Oli to resign, prompting an interim government under Sushila Karki, a former Chief Justice, to organise fresh polls. The result surprised even close observers of Nepali politics: the Rastriya Swatantra Party, founded only in 2022 by broadcaster-turned-politician Rabi Lamichhane and now led by former Kathmandu mayor Balendra 'Balen' Shah, won 182 of the 275 seats in the House of Representatives, an outright majority. The Nepali Congress, one of Nepal's two traditional dominant parties, came a distant second with 38 seats, and Oli's own Communist Party of Nepal (Unified Marxist-Leninist) took just 25. It was the first time since 1999 that a single party had secured a parliamentary majority in Nepal on its own.

Balen Shah, a rapper and structural engineer before becoming Kathmandu's independent mayor in 2022, was sworn in as prime minister on 27 March, eight days after the final results were confirmed. His cabinet, sworn in the same day, is the youngest in Nepal's history, and only two of its members carry prior ministerial experience.

Nepal abolished its 240-year-old monarchy in 2008, after a decade-long Maoist insurgency, becoming a federal democratic republic; its current constitution, promulgated in 2015, established the 275-seat House elected through a mixed system of first-past-the-post and proportional representation. Since 2015, Nepal had cycled through numerous short-lived coalition governments, which is the backdrop against which the RSP's outright win looks so unusual.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: The abolition of Nepal's monarchy in 2008
The Rastriya Swatantra Party's landslide election win and Balen Shah becoming Nepal's Prime Minister
A conflict between Nepal and India over their shared border
The Nepali Congress winning a majority government
questions.explain: The passage's main subject is the RSP's outright majority win in the March 2026 election and Balen Shah's swearing-in as Prime Minister. The monarchy's abolition is mentioned only as background context, there is no India-Nepal border conflict discussed, and it was the RSP, not the Nepali Congress, that won a majority.

questions.q: According to the passage, what triggered Nepal's March 2026 election?
options: A scheduled election under the 2015 constitution's normal five-year cycle
Youth-led protests in September 2025 that forced PM Oli's resignation
A Supreme Court order dissolving Parliament
An agreement between the Nepali Congress and CPN-UML to hold early polls
questions.explain: The passage states the election 'followed directly from the political rupture of September 2025, when youth-led street protests forced Prime Minister K.P. Sharma Oli to resign.' No court order or inter-party agreement is mentioned as the trigger.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is true based on the passage?
options: The RSP was founded in 1999
Sushila Karki was sworn in as Nepal's permanent Prime Minister after the election
This was the first time since 1999 that a single party won a parliamentary majority in Nepal
Balen Shah had significant prior ministerial experience before becoming PM
questions.explain: The passage states directly: 'It was the first time since 1999 that a single party had secured a parliamentary majority in Nepal on its own.' The RSP was founded in 2022, not 1999; Karki led only the interim government, not a permanent one; and Balen Shah's background was as a mayor, rapper, and engineer, not a minister.

questions.q: The passage's mention of Nepal's 'numerous short-lived coalition governments' since 2015 mainly serves to:
options: Criticise the 2015 constitution as poorly written
Explain why the RSP's outright majority is being treated as an unusual and significant result
Argue that Nepal should return to a monarchy
Suggest that Nepal has never had a stable government in its entire history
questions.explain: The passage uses this detail specifically to contextualise why the RSP's win 'looks so unusual' against a backdrop of unstable coalitions. It does not criticise the constitution's drafting, argue for monarchy's return, or make a claim about all of Nepali history.

questions.q: A student who knows that Nepal shares an open border with India would most reasonably connect that fact to which idea suggested by the passage?
options: That Nepal's internal election results have no bearing on India at all
That a new, untested government in Kathmandu is likely to be closely watched by India given how closely the two countries' politics and people are linked
That India directly controls Nepal's electoral process
That the open border was created because of the 2015 constitution
questions.explain: Given how closely India and Nepal's societies and economies are intertwined through an open border, a change in Nepal's ruling party is naturally something India would track closely, an inference the passage supports without stating outright. The other options go well beyond, or against, what the passage and general knowledge support.

passages.title: Why the Rajya Sabha couldn't stop the Finance Bill
passages.passage:
India's Budget Session ran from 28 January to 2 April 2026, split into two phases with a recess in between for parliamentary committees to scrutinise the government's spending proposals. The Lok Sabha resumed discussion on the Finance Bill 2026 on 24 March and passed it by voice vote the next day. The Bill then went to the Rajya Sabha, which, unlike with an ordinary piece of legislation, could not amend it directly.

The reason lies in how the Constitution classifies certain bills. Article 110 defines a Money Bill as one dealing exclusively with taxation, government borrowing, or the custody of the Consolidated Fund of India, and gives the Speaker of the Lok Sabha final, uncontestable authority to certify whether a given bill qualifies. Article 109 then lays out a special procedure for any bill so certified: it must originate in the Lok Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha has only fourteen days to return it with recommendations, which the Lok Sabha is free to accept or reject outright. This is why India's upper house, despite representing the states, has essentially no veto over the country's tax and spending decisions once a bill carries the Speaker's Money Bill certification.

Not every bill introduced in the same session moves this fast. A separate Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026, introduced by Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman on 23 March, was referred to a Joint Parliamentary Committee for clause-by-clause examination rather than passed outright, since it did not carry a Money Bill certification and Parliament chose to route it through a slower consultative process instead. The Finance Bill also completed the phase-out of the GST compensation cess, a levy introduced in 2017 to compensate states for revenue lost during the transition to GST, and Parliament separately passed Appropriation Bills authorising the government to actually withdraw the funds Parliament had already approved through the Demands for Grants process.

questions.q: What is the main point the passage makes about the Rajya Sabha's role in passing the Finance Bill 2026?
options: The Rajya Sabha rejected the Bill outright
The Rajya Sabha could only recommend changes within 14 days, which the Lok Sabha was free to ignore
The Rajya Sabha has equal power to the Lok Sabha over all financial legislation
The Rajya Sabha did not discuss the Bill at all
questions.explain: The passage explains that under Article 109, the Rajya Sabha's role on a certified Money Bill is limited to recommending changes within 14 days, changes the Lok Sabha can reject entirely. It does not say the Rajya Sabha rejected the Bill, nor does it claim equal power between the Houses, nor that there was no discussion at all.

questions.q: According to the passage, what determines whether a bill is treated as a Money Bill?
options: A vote of both Houses of Parliament
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha's certification, which is final and not open to challenge
The President's discretion
Whether the Finance Minister personally introduces the bill
questions.explain: The passage states Article 110 'gives the Speaker of the Lok Sabha final, uncontestable authority to certify whether a given bill qualifies' as a Money Bill. No joint vote, presidential discretion, or rule about who introduces the bill is mentioned as the determining factor.

questions.q: Which of the following is true, based on the passage?
options: The Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 was certified as a Money Bill
The GST compensation cess was introduced in 2017 and its phase-out was completed around the Finance Bill 2026
The Rajya Sabha has an unlimited amount of time to consider a Money Bill
The Budget Session in 2026 had no recess between its two phases
questions.explain: The passage states the GST compensation cess was 'introduced in 2017' and that its phase-out was completed as part of Finance Bill 2026. The Corporate Laws Bill was explicitly not treated as a Money Bill (it went to a JPC instead); the Rajya Sabha's window is 14 days, not unlimited; and the session did have a recess between phases, per the passage's opening line.

questions.q: The passage's comparison between the Finance Bill and the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill mainly illustrates that:
options: All bills introduced by the Finance Minister automatically become Money Bills
The pace and procedure a bill follows through Parliament depends on its legal classification, not simply on which minister introduces it
The Rajya Sabha always sends bills to a Joint Parliamentary Committee
Money Bills and ordinary bills are processed identically
questions.explain: Both bills were introduced by the same minister in the same session, yet one moved swiftly as a certified Money Bill while the other went to a JPC, illustrating that classification, not the introducing minister, drives the process. This directly contradicts options A and D, and the JPC referral in this case wasn't a general Rajya Sabha practice, as option C claims.

questions.q: A student who separately knows that Article 114 governs Appropriation Bills would use that knowledge to understand that, unlike the Finance Bill described in the passage, an Appropriation Bill:
options: Introduces new taxes not previously approved
Authorises withdrawal of funds from the Consolidated Fund for expenditure Parliament has already voted on, rather than setting new tax policy
Cannot be passed in the same session as a Finance Bill
Is not related to the Union Budget process at all
questions.explain: Combining the passage's own mention of Appropriation Bills 'authorising the government to actually withdraw the funds Parliament had already approved' with outside knowledge of Article 114 clarifies the distinction from the Finance Bill: an Appropriation Bill executes already-approved spending, while the Finance Bill sets substantive tax policy. Both bills were in fact passed in the same session, and both are integral, not unrelated, to the Budget process.

passages.title: Legislating over a constitutional right
passages.passage:
The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, 2026 was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 13 March 2026, passed there by voice vote on 24 March, cleared the Rajya Sabha the next day, and received presidential assent on 30 March, moving from introduction to law in roughly seventeen days. It amends the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019, itself controversial for requiring transgender persons to obtain a District Magistrate's certificate before their gender identity could be officially recognised, a requirement critics said already contradicted the spirit of an earlier Supreme Court ruling.

That ruling, NALSA v Union of India, decided in 2014, is the doctrinal starting point for any analysis of this Bill. A two-judge bench held that the right to self-identify one's gender, without any external medical or administrative certification, flows directly from Article 21's guarantee of dignity, alongside Articles 14 and 15. NALSA also directed the state to treat transgender persons as a distinct 'third gender' and extend reservations in education and public employment comparable to those available to other backward classes.

The 2026 amendment moves further in the direction the 2019 Act had already been criticised for. It redefines the statutory category of 'transgender' more narrowly, removes references to self-perceived gender identity altogether, and excludes several socio-cultural identities, including trans-masculine individuals, from the Act's protection. The government's stated justification was closing definitional ambiguity that made welfare-scheme implementation difficult; opposition MPs argued the Bill should have gone to a Standing Committee for wider consultation given how directly it touched a right the Supreme Court had already recognised. Amnesty International called the amendment's presidential approval 'a major step backward for human rights,' and Human Rights Watch described it as a significant setback for India's transgender community.

questions.q: What is the central tension the passage describes?
options: A dispute between the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha over procedure
A conflict between a right the Supreme Court recognised in NALSA (2014) and a narrower definition Parliament has now legislated
A disagreement over whether India should have a Transgender Persons Act at all
A dispute between Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch
questions.explain: The passage's throughline is the gap between the self-identification right NALSA (2014) established under Article 21 and the narrower statutory definition the 2026 amendment now enacts. There is no Lok Sabha-Rajya Sabha procedural conflict described (the Bill passed both without incident), no dispute over having an Act at all, and Amnesty and HRW are described as agreeing, not disagreeing, in their criticism.

questions.q: According to the passage, what did NALSA v Union of India (2014) establish?
options: A requirement that transgender persons obtain a District Magistrate's certificate
That the right to self-identify one's gender flows from Article 21, alongside Articles 14 and 15
The current definition used in the 2026 Amendment Bill
That transgender persons cannot be given reservations in employment
questions.explain: The passage states NALSA held self-identification 'flows directly from Article 21's guarantee of dignity, alongside Articles 14 and 15.' The DM-certificate requirement came later, in the 2019 Act, and directly contradicted NALSA's spirit rather than being established by it; NALSA also directed reservations be extended, the opposite of option D.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is true, based on the passage?
options: The 2026 Amendment Bill received presidential assent on 13 March 2026
The 2019 Act required no certification for gender recognition
NALSA v Union of India was decided by a nine-judge bench
The Bill moved from introduction to presidential assent in roughly seventeen days
questions.explain: The passage states the Bill was introduced 13 March and received assent 30 March, 'roughly seventeen days.' Presidential assent came on 30 March, not 13 March (the introduction date); the 2019 Act did require a DM certificate, contrary to option B; and NALSA was decided by a two-judge bench, not nine, per the passage.

questions.q: The passage's mention of opposition MPs wanting a Standing Committee referral mainly illustrates that:
options: The Bill was entirely uncontroversial and passed without any objection
Some legislators believed a Bill touching a previously recognised constitutional right deserved more deliberation than roughly seventeen days allowed
The Standing Committee has the power to strike down unconstitutional bills
The Rajya Sabha refused to vote on the Bill
questions.explain: The detail about opposition MPs seeking Standing Committee referral illustrates a concern about the speed and depth of scrutiny given the Bill's significance, not that the Bill was uncontroversial (it clearly was not) or that the Rajya Sabha refused to vote (the passage says it 'cleared the Rajya Sabha'). A Standing Committee also has no power to strike down legislation; only courts can do that.

questions.q: A student who knows India has no formal mechanism for Parliament to overrule a Supreme Court constitutional interpretation, short of a constitutional amendment, would most reasonably conclude that:
options: The 2026 Amendment automatically overrules NALSA and cannot be challenged
A statute narrowing a right the Court has read into Article 21 remains open to future constitutional challenge before the Court
NALSA is no longer valid law now that the 2026 Amendment exists
Parliament needed a two-thirds majority to pass the 2026 Amendment because it touches a fundamental right
questions.explain: Since ordinary legislation cannot override a constitutional right the Supreme Court has recognised, a law narrowing that right remains vulnerable to being challenged and potentially struck down by the same Court, which is the logical implication the outside knowledge supports. NALSA remains valid precedent unless and until a court says otherwise, and the passage gives no indication a special majority was required or used.
